How to Connect Accessibility Metrics to Organizational Outcomes

Sep 21, 2026

Author: Level Access

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:04
Instaread

Maybe your teams have already audited your digital portfolio, fixed critical issues, or been trained on accessibility standards. Or maybe you’re just getting started. Either way, you’ve probably found yourself fielding questions from leaders that don’t have easy answers. Legal wants to know if accessibility-related risk is falling. Sales needs a current conformance report for a buyer conversation. Stakeholders want to understand whether their investment in accessibility is paying off.

Are you able to answer quickly, with evidence already at hand, or do you have to scramble to assemble the data?

No matter where you are on your accessibility journey, this blog explains how to connect your work to four outcomes leaders commonly track: regulatory risk, cost and efficiency, revenue readiness, and customer experience.

What happens when impact isn’t clear?

When accessibility work isn’t connected to organizational outcomes, it can be hard to explain why it matters or get the resources you need to sustain progress. Unfortunately, this is one of the most common sticking points for teams at every stage. In fact, professionals surveyed for our latest State of Digital Accessibility Report were most likely to rank competing organizational priorities among the top three challenges facing their program.

The best way to solve for this problem (or even better, stay ahead of it) is to clearly map the accessibility work you’re doing to the results that matter to leaders.

Where to start: Establish your baseline

A useful starting point is to ask yourself what a leader or stakeholder has asked you recently. Were they worried about legal exposure? Trying to understand how your accessibility team works? Asking for documentation to share with a buyer? That question should help you understand what kind of evidence you need to build.

Once you’ve identified your question, establish your baseline: what you’re measuring and why. It doesn’t need to be elaborate. A conformance score, open issues, properties tested. Anything that shows your starting point. That’s what you measure future progress against.

A framework such as the Digital Accessibility Maturity Model (DAMM™) can help by giving you a program-level benchmark and direction on where to focus next. Take our free Digital Accessibility Maturity Quick Check to get an initial benchmark in just a few minutes.

How to map accessibility metrics to outcomes

With a solid baseline, you can track the accessibility progress your team is making over time. But chances are, your leaders don’t track the same accessibility metrics you do. The problems they care about are higher-level: risk, efficiency, revenue, and customer experience.

Let’s explore how you can connect your work to each of these in three steps: building the evidence, demonstrating the outcome, and putting the evidence to work.

Legal and regulatory risk

How exposed are we to a demand letter, lawsuit, or regulatory complaint? Is it getting better or worse? Most leaders start with these questions. You don’t need legal expertise to answer them.

Build the evidence

Start with the risk signals you already have: customer complaints about accessibility, support tickets mentioning barriers, and legal inquiries or demand letters. Even the absence of these tells a story. From there, connect those signals to the accessibility data that might explain them. That might include critical barriers across your portfolio, the rate of new issues versus fixes, and which properties you’re testing.

If you don’t have any of those, that’s worth noting too. It may mean your testing coverage is low, not that your risk is.

Demonstrate the outcome

You’ll know risk is falling when you notice critical barriers disappearing from high-traffic journeys with each release, and your testing coverage is expanding to the places most likely to spark complaints. The trend matters more than any single number.

Put the evidence to work

Different stakeholders often need different cuts of the same evidence. An engineering manager might want a weekly summary of unresolved findings to improve delivery, while an accessibility champion may need a monthly progress report for leadership.

Level Access’s Reporting Agent brings accessibility data from websites, applications, and documents into one reporting system. Teams can build and schedule reports around the questions different stakeholders are asking and connect that activity to risk reduction over time.

Risk usually gets leaders’ attention first. Once that conversation is underway, the next question is usually: Is this getting easier to manage?

Cost and operational efficiency

Accessibility work costs time and money. Finding issues late, reworking code after release, and replacing vendor components that don’t meet requirements are all operational costs—even if they don’t always get labeled as accessibility expenses.

Build the evidence

Start by identifying where accessibility is already creating friction. Are developers fixing things post-launch that could have been caught earlier? Are releases getting delayed? Those patterns are the beginning of a cost story.

Then pair them with data. What proportion of issues are caught before release? How many findings trace back to shared design system components? A barrier in a shared component can show up across every product that uses it. Fix it once and you remove it everywhere.

Demonstrate the outcome

Teams that catch issues in the design phase instead of after shipping cut rework time per cycle. Repeat barriers falling means you stop fixing the same problems across every product. Accessibility baked into vendor contracts eliminates the cost of swapping components mid-project. When design checks become standard, when you’ve defined accessibility owners, and when requirements live in contracts, rework drops, costs drop, and you’re no longer fixing the same barrier in multiple products.

Put the evidence to work

Finance and engineering leaders will want the cost story, not just the issue count. Report the proportion of issues caught before release alongside the rework it avoided. Pair that with component-level trends, so the leader can better understand where prevention is making a difference.

Tools like Level CI run accessibility checks against pull requests, so developers can understand the accessibility impact of a change (and a suggested fix) before it merges. That keeps issues out of production, without slowing delivery.

If efficiency is starting to improve, that may be a sign accessibility is becoming part of how the organization works. The next question is whether it’s also helping the business grow.

Revenue and procurement readiness

Accessibility influences both consumer and business-to-business (B2B) sales. In fact, 77% of professionals surveyed for our State of Digital Accessibility Report said accessibility improvements contributed to stronger revenue. Here’s how to prove it.

Build the evidence

For customer journeys such as checkout, applications, account creation, and renewals, focus on where people abandon tasks, need help to complete them, or call support instead. If you can cross-reference those drop-off points with known accessibility barriers, you should be able to pinpoint where the experience is losing people.

In B2B and business-to-government (B2G) sales, the pressure often surfaces during procurement. Buyers, particularly in government and regulated industries, might ask for an accessibility conformance report (ACR), a document that describes how well your product meets accessibility standards. If you don’t have one, or yours is out of date, that can create friction at exactly the wrong moment. Whether you’re starting with your first ACR or refining your fifth, buyers evaluate the same things: Is it current? Does it cover what we’re evaluating? Can you back it up?

Demonstrate the outcome

Revenue grows when checkout, applications, and renewals have fewer drop-offs tied to accessibility barriers. Support costs drop when the experience works for everyone.

In procurement, deals move when you have a current, comprehensive ACR that buyers trust. The outcome: Accessibility stops being friction in sales and starts being a competitive asset.

Put the evidence to work

When customer journeys become more accessible over time, it’ll become clear in lower support costs, higher completion rates, and fewer abandoned transactions. Procurement evidence will help you get past the evaluation phase with more buyers.

Customer experience and usability

Whether it’s checkout, application submission, or account renewal, there’s a version of that experience that works for users. There’s also a version that loses them. The question is: Which one are you providing?

Build the evidence

Complaints and support data can point you toward problems, but they only capture the people who reported an issue. And not every user will. Instead, they’ll abandon the task, find a workaround, or simply won’t come back.

Testing with people who regularly use assistive technology gives you a clearer picture of what the experience is actually like. It doesn’t require a large study. Even a small number of sessions can surface barriers that automated testing and manual audits miss. If you’re not doing this yet, it’s worth exploring.

Demonstrate the outcome

You’re making progress when more people complete important tasks independently and recurring barriers drop across critical journeys. But completion isn’t the full picture. Capture whether people struggled, asked for help, or had to find workarounds. That context should help you identify what to fix next.

Put the evidence to work

Bringing people with disabilities into testing early is often more useful than waiting until the end of the process. Feedback at that stage can reveal the next barrier as quickly as it validates the one you’ve removed, giving teams a clearer understanding of where to focus.

Over time, that builds a picture of which journeys are improving, where people are still being excluded, and what to address next.

Prove accessibility matters to the business

Leaders rarely ask for accessibility metrics. They ask about risk, efficiency, revenue, and customer experience. When you connect accessibility work to outcomes, you’re no longer explaining how accessibility impacts the organization—you’re proving it does.

Backed by 25 years of accessibility expertise, Level Access consolidates your fragmented accessibility data into one platform, giving you the evidence to reduce risk, close deals faster, and demonstrate the business impact that keeps accessibility funded.

Ready to connect your accessibility work to outcomes that matter?
